posts.author: Cristiano_Perrucci
posts.content_md:
Hi all,

After a forced long time of inactivity, last night I put hands in my chemicals box and I prepared 5 MBDCG plates.

Now, I do have a question concerning red sensitive DCG homebrew plates.

Reading the original paper of prof. Blyth, I found that emulsion sensitivity is dramatically influenced by gel moisture. It seems that the best results are achieved around 66% of Relative Humidity, while below 33% RH plates becomes unusable.

Is this a one way process or dried plates (RH below 33%) may be brought back to working conditions just rising the relative humidity?

Thanks,

Cristiano, IT

posts.author: jeff-blyth
posts.content_md:
> **Cristiano_Perrucci:** Hi all,After a forced long time of inactivity, last night I put hands in my chemicals box and I prepared 5 MBDCG plates.Now, I do have a question concerning red sensitive DCG homebrew plates.Reading the original paper of prof. Blyth, I found that emulsion sensitivity is dramatically influenced by gel moisture. It seems that the best results are achieved around 66% of Relative Humidity, while below 33% RH plates becomes unusable.Is this a one way process or dried plates (RH below 33%) may be brought back to working conditions just rising the relative humidity?Thanks,Cristiano, IT

Yes of course they can become resensitized by higher humidity Cristiano,

it puzzles me on what basis you could have thought otherwise.

Keeping unexposed plates very dry is a good way to extend their effective lifetimes which are much longer than standard dichromate plates anyway.

Once you have rehumidified them it is a good idea to lock that moisture level up in a glass sandwich and allow a good settling time before shooting.

Jeff

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Jeff, I never thought "locking" in the moisture with a glass sandwich was necessary. I think that once the plate is remoisturized then they would be good for hours as the moisture evaporates slowly. Is this not the case? Does old dried out and remoisturized gelatin lose water more quickly then fresh plates?

The reason I ask is I am thinking of the negatives of pulling off the glass cover after exposure and prior to processing an wet and thus softened gelatin.

John

posts.author: jeff-blyth
posts.content_md:
> **JohnFP:** Jeff, I never thought "locking" in the moisture with a glass sandwich was necessary. I think that once the plate is remoisturized then they would be good for hours as the moisture evaporates slowly. Is this not the case? Does old dried out and remoisturized gelatin lose water more quickly then fresh plates?The reason I ask is I am thinking of the negatives of pulling off the glass cover after exposure and prior to processing an wet and thus softened gelatin.John

Yes that is a very good point John, but the thing about the MBDCG system is that it is more moist and has an appreciable bit of the amine TMG which also acts as a humectant. This makes it less difficult to remove a cover plate. From your stand point it would be better to use a very thin 

clear isotropic plastic film, like the covering on a newly opened pot of jam!

jeff

posts.author: Cristiano_Perrucci
posts.content_md:
Oh Jeff... thanks for your answer.

Would you like to know why this question so obvious? because working with DCG and related items, reminds me a walk on thin ice (eg. possible TMG release when dry and so on). 

So before starting I want to be sure to make the right thing.

Again thanks,

Cristiano, IT

posts.author: Tom B.
posts.content_md:
> **jeff-blyth:** Yes of course they can become resensitized by higher humidity Cristiano,it puzzles me on what basis you could have thought otherwise.

I think he may have been thinking of the many things which cannot be restored to their fresh state by rehumidifying after they have been dessicated - for example bread, tobacco, fruit, Egyptian mummies ... most organic things in fact. Fortunately it seems that MBDCG is not among them.
